The cross-group real-earnings growth spread narrowed slightly to 3.0 percentage points. macro.body: Market performance has strengthened while hardware production continues to expand. The AI Equity Index increased materially to 35.6 and the median one-year return rose to 11.4%, although positive-return breadth eased to 60.3%. Semiconductor and electronic-component output is growing 19.9%, far faster than computer and peripheral-equipment output at 6.5%. Reuters reported that Anthropic’s IPO filing lifted AI stocks while drawing attention to the company’s rapid growth and escalating costs. The combined picture is one of sustained appetite for AI exposure, but not a uniform improvement across companies or a resolution of the sector’s economics. The buildout is also meeting a more demanding power environment. Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, compared with 1.8% for total retail demand, and retail prices are up 5.1%; each accelerated materially. Supply pipelines appear large on separate measures: net planned generation additions total 227.6 GW, while active interconnection queues contain 2,061 GW. Yet only 24.2% of the queue has reached an executed agreement or construction, and historically 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation. These figures do not attribute rising demand or prices to AI, but they show why planned capacity should not be treated as power already available to new computing loads. The labor signals remain considerably narrower. Only one tracked AI-linked channel is adding jobs; power and communication construction leads at 0.8%, while two channels have positive real-earnings growth. Reuters also reported job cuts as companies shift investment toward AI, including a planned 5,000-role reduction at Barclays. Economy-wide productivity and real output are growing 2.2% and 2.5%, respectively, but real hourly compensation growth is 0.6%. Those aggregate outcomes cannot isolate AI’s contribution, and they have not coincided with broad employment growth across the tracked channels.
macro.headline: Market gains and chip output remain strong as power demand accelerates and job growth stays narrow

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

body.text: The AI Equity Index rose materially to 38.2, while the median one-year return climbed to 13.8% and the equal-weight return edged up to 21.3%. Average sector trading pressure slipped slightly to 47.9, so the stronger trailing performance has not coincided with more intense trading pressure. Investor’s Business Daily reported that an Nvidia partner rallied after strong earnings and guidance; Reuters separately described Anthropic’s rapid sales growth and steep losses as a test for its IPO. The contrast illustrates why strong demand for AI exposure can coexist with sharply different underlying economics.

body.text: The Chicago Fed NFCI stands at -0.49 after rising 0.04 over three months. Lender strain increased slightly to 17.4, and corporate bond-market distress edged up to 0.25. These measures point in the same direction at the margin, but not with the same intensity. The Financial Times reported a surge in default-insurance trading tied to AI debt concerns, while Morningstar reported a $40 billion GPU leasing deal involving SpaceX and private-credit firms. The reports show that very large AI-related financing and greater trading in credit protection can occur at the same time; they do not establish broad credit deterioration by themselves.

headline.text: Credit indicators edge toward greater strain even as private credit funds a large GPU deal

body.text: Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, nearly twice the 1.8% increase in total retail demand, while retail electricity prices are up 5.1%. Net planned generation additions total 227.6 GW, but they remain pipeline capacity rather than operating supply. Utility Dive reported on Google’s virtual power plant in PJM in the context of intensifying competition for electricity. The project adds a nontraditional response to the power challenge, although the reported development does not show its scale or whether it can materially ease supply pressure. The figures also do not establish AI as the cause of broader demand or price growth.

body.text: Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% alongside a 2.5% increase in real output, while real hourly compensation rose 0.6%. Unit labor costs increased 1.4%. The pattern shows broad productivity gains without a comparable rise in real hourly compensation, but it does not identify the source of those gains. Axios reported skepticism that AI is yet adding much to productivity. That report is consistent with the attribution problem in the aggregate data, not proof that AI has had no effect.

headline.text: Productivity growth outpaces real compensation, but AI’s contribution remains unclear
AI equity gains strengthen as debt exposure and power-delivery risk come into clearer view

paragraphs.text: AI equity performance has strengthened across more than one measure. The AI Equity Index rose materially to 38.2, the median one-year return reached 13.8%, and the equal-weight return edged up to 21.3%. Investor’s Business Daily reported that an Nvidia partner surged after strong earnings and guidance, while Reuters highlighted Anthropic’s combination of rapid sales growth and steep losses ahead of an IPO. Investors are still rewarding AI exposure, but those examples underscore that supplier earnings and model-company economics remain very different propositions.

The financing system can support very large commitments, though its direction has become somewhat less favorable. The Chicago Fed NFCI rose 0.04 over three months to -0.49, while lender strain and corporate bond distress both edged higher. Morningstar reported a $40 billion GPU leasing deal involving SpaceX and private credit, and the Financial Times reported a surge in default-insurance trading amid AI debt concerns. Large financing capacity and increased credit hedging are visible at the same time; neither report demonstrates system-wide distress.

Power remains the clearest physical execution issue. Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, faster than total retail demand at 1.8%, and retail prices are up 5.1%. Supply pipelines look large on separate measures: net planned generation additions total 227.6 GW, and active interconnection queues contain 2,061 GW. Yet only 24.2% of the queue is in executed-agreement or construction stages, and 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation. Utility Dive’s report on Google’s virtual power plant in PJM shows one company pursuing another route while new generation works through the pipeline. The central distinction remains between announced capacity and power that can actually serve load.

The macroeconomic return remains harder to identify than the investment itself. Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% and real output 2.5%, but real hourly compensation rose 0.6% and unit labor costs 1.4%. Business adoption is still partial: 24.6% report current AI use and 28.6% expect to use it within six months, compared with 60.8% of adults ages 18–64 reporting some generative-AI use. These figures show broad consumer use and narrower business deployment, but they cannot isolate AI’s contribution to productivity or compensation.
